conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a clinician who specializes in helping new moms navigate the emotional ups and downs that can come after having a baby. I’ll be guiding you through a short, well-trusted questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**—or “EPDS” for short. It’s simply a 10-question check-in that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling in the past week so we can make sure you’re getting any support you might need.

Everything you share stays completely confidential between you and our care team, and there are no right or wrong answers. We just want to hear your honest experience so we can best support you and your family. When you’re ready, we’ll move through the questions one by one; each should only take a moment.

Let’s start:  
Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

Honestly… most of the time it feels kind of hard. My husband will make a joke or I’ll see something on my phone that normally would’ve made me giggle, but lately it just falls flat—like I have to force it. I did laugh once when the baby made a silly face mid-burp, but even then the happy feeling faded right away and I felt tired again.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not really… I’d say most days this week I couldn’t. I laughed once, maybe twice, but it felt forced—like I was doing it because I “should,” not because anything felt genuinely funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not much at all. I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but this week nothing really feels worth looking forward to. I still do the things because I know I should, but the whole time I’m just kind of… flat.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If the baby’s fussy, I immediately think it must be something I ate or that I’m not soothing him right. Yesterday he wouldn’t nap and I kept replaying every single thing I did, convinced it was my fault for holding him “wrong” or not reading his cues fast enough. Even when my husband says “babies just cry,” I still feel like I’m failing somehow.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding him and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure he’s not gaining enough weight, even though the pediatrician said he’s perfect. Last night I kept checking if he was breathing every ten minutes. I know in my head it’s unlikely anything bad will happen, but I can’t shake the “what-ifs.”
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not full-blown panic, but I get these sudden waves of fear, like something awful’s about to happen. Yesterday, just sitting on the couch, my chest got tight and I felt like I couldn’t get a deep breath. It passed after a few minutes, but it left me shaky and on edge the rest of the afternoon.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… most days it feels like I’m drowning in small stuff. Dishes pile up, the baby needs changing, I haven’t showered, and suddenly I’m sitting on the kitchen floor crying because it all feels impossible. I do manage to get through it, but I’m constantly playing catch-up and never feel on top of anything.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah, that’s been happening almost every night this week. I lie down exhausted, but my mind just keeps spinning—replaying everything I think I did wrong, worrying about the baby, feeling guilty that I’m not happier. I’ll finally drift off around 2 a.m. and then I’m up again when he cries at 3:30. Even when he settles, I can’t get back to sleep; I just stare at the ceiling feeling sad and tense until morning.
I have felt sad or miserable

Most of the time, yeah. It’s like there’s a heaviness that won’t lift. I’ll be rocking the baby and tears just start slipping out for no clear reason. I keep thinking I should feel grateful—he’s healthy, my husband’s helping—but the sadness is still there anyway.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… I’ve cried three times this week. Once was right after the pediatrician visit—everything went fine, but when I got to the car I just burst into tears. Another night I was folding tiny onesies and started sobbing because it hit me how much I love him and how scared I am that I’m not enough for him. The tears come out of nowhere and once they start it’s hard to stop.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… I haven’t had any thoughts like that. I feel overwhelmed and sad, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom my baby needs.

You've shared that the past week has felt overwhelmingly heavy: most days you can't find real joy or laughter, everything feels flat, and ordinary tasks seem impossible. Nights are especially hard-your mind races with worries and guilt while the rest of the house sleeps-and tears arrive without warning. Even when good things happen, like a healthy check-up for your baby, the sadness quickly takes over again.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports inability to laugh naturally, only forced attempts—aligns with "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes near-complete loss of anticipatory joy, aligning with "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient endorses frequent, pervasive self-blame even when others reassure her, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily, intrusive worries without clear cause, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden waves of fear and physical symptoms (tight chest, breathlessness) consistent with episodic anxiety, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily overwhelm, inability to manage routine tasks, and emotional collapse, aligning with "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly sleep disturbance driven by unhappiness, rumination, and guilt, matching 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports sadness "most of the time" plus persistent heaviness and unexplained crying spells, aligning with "Yes, most of the time".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple crying episodes triggered by everyday moments, indicating frequent emotional distress.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 25 places you well above the threshold indicating probable <med>major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>. You endorsed frequent or constant difficulty with enjoyment, laughter, sleep, overwhelming feelings, and spontaneous crying, meeting core DSM-5 mood-episode criteria. Your description of sudden chest tightness and fear also suggests co-occurring <med>anxiety</med>. Safety screening was negative, which is reassuring, yet symptom severity still warrants prompt clinical attention. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange an urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med> or a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> to review these results
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med>, peer support groups, or <med>antidepressant medication</med> compatible with breastfeeding if desired
3. Involve a trusted support person in planning so daily tasks feel less overwhelming
4. Use brief mood or EPDS self-checks weekly to track changes and share with providers
5. Practice small, manageable self-care steps-hydration, 5-minute outdoor light exposure, accepting help with chores-and celebrate any progress
6. Keep national resources handy: Postpartum Support International (1-800-944-4773) or the National Maternal Mental Health Hotline (1-833-943-5746) for 24/7 support
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: **Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary**  
*(Patient: 1–2 wks postpartum; responses to 10-item EPDS analog)*

**Symptoms endorsed**  
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness  
- Marked anhedonia (loss of interest/pleasure)  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame regarding infant care  
- Multiple daily worries, “what-ifs,” nocturnal rumination  
- Episodic chest tightness, breathlessness, fear flashes (sub-panic)  
- Feeling overwhelmed, “drowning,” functional tasks “impossible”  
- Initial and middle insomnia (2 a.m. onset, difficulty re-settling)  
- No self-harm ideation (explicitly denied)

**Patterns / Risk indicators**  
- Symptoms present nearly every day for the past week, causing subjective distress and interference with basic ADLs  
- Sleep disruption linked to mood rather than infant schedule alone  
- High self-criticism and maternal self-efficacy concerns  
- No psychotic features; no suicidal thoughts (protective factor)

**Screening significance**  
- Score profile consistent with probable major depressive episode with co-occurring anxiety (postpartum onset)  
- Recommends: formal clinical interview (DSM-5-TR criteria), standardized EPDS scoring, differential for GAD, panic spectrum, and postpartum anxiety disorders  
- Safety: no current self-harm risk; continue routine safety monitoring

**Next steps documented for provider review**
